extracted.intended_audience: trial judges and patent litigators (trial counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical recommendations and courtroom standards for conducting patent jury trials to maximize juror comprehension and trial quality (covers bifurcation, voir dire, evidence presentation, jury instructions, verdict forms, and the division of legal vs. factual issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose jury instructions at pretrial conference
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial counsel might consider offering jury instructions to the judge at the pretrial conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accompany proposed instructions with a proposed verdict form; early submission helps focus issues for trial (see references to SRI Int'l and Judge Cohn's practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider bifurcating the trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider separating issues (e.g., damages vs. liability, willfulness, antitrust counterclaims) into separate phases or trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bifurcation is not barred by the Seventh Amendment and courts have granted and denied such motions. Advantages: reduces overlapping evidence and may improve juror comprehension; courts may conduct multi-phase trials with the same jury. Disadvantages: creates piecemeal quality, may prevent jurors from seeing the case as a whole, may foster overemphasis on particular issues. Only recommend bifurcation when there is a clearly separable issue that would control the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try one major issue at a time
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider trying a single major issue in each phase (even without formal bifurcation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although historically some proposed trying infringement first then validity only if infringement found, both issues must be dealt with (Cardinal Chemical). Other helpful separations: different patents separately, different claims separately, and separating method claims from apparatus claims. Bellwether/batch trials on particular issues may define conclusions for separated issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precharge the jury with legal and technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain legal and technical terms (e.g., obviousness, anticipation, infringement) in preliminary instructions and provide written versions as references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should hear terms in preliminary instructions, receive them in writing, and keep written copies during trial to enhance comprehension; see Plain English Instructions in Appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose fair and reasonable time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Set and enforce time limits for each side's use of direct and cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult with counsel to allocate a set number of hours for each side and hold parties to those limits to keep trial focused and manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number of expert witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presenting multiple experts who cover the same ground, especially when one expert corrects another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple experts often lead to confusion; limit redundant expert testimony to improve clarity for jurors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use jury questionnaires for voir dire
rubrics_metrics.description: Have venire members complete questionnaires returned to judge and counsel before oral voir dire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questionnaires allow for pre-screening (for cause) and, when combined with expanded voir dire or attorney-conducted voir dire, are especially valuable in technically complex cases to select able jurors and allow attorneys to assess rapport for peremptory use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider nonrandom seating selection from the venire
rubrics_metrics.description: After voir dire, the judge may select a sufficient number of prospective jurors based on case-relevant criteria and seat them after chambers conferences with counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'extra-qualified jury' approach can have advantages (selecting jurors suited to complex cases) but risks bias; retain challenges for cause and peremptory challenges. Another method (with consent) allows each counsel to pick half the necessary jurors from the venire subject to challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage use of visual aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote charts, diagrams, maps, enlarged photographs, models, and videotapes to aid juror comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual aids help explain technical evidence; see SRI Int'l and Schwarzer recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider mounting witness photographs in courtroom
rubrics_metrics.description: Post enlarged photographs of witnesses to help jurors remember testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to aid juror memory over multi-day trials or many witnesses (Schwarzer's recommendation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude marginally probative evidence likely to confuse jurors
rubrics_metrics.description: Refuse to admit written material or exhibits that jurors cannot reasonably read/absorb, or that are marginally probative and likely to confuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use summaries and excerpts where possible; provide jurors with finding aids for exhibits that must be received in full; court should limit written material to what a juror could absorb within an hour or two (Schwarzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain English
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate with jurors in plain English and avoid legalese.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain language improves comprehension; use concrete words, avoid homonyms, avoid negative modifiers, prefer simple grammar and clear organization; specific words to avoid include 'plaintiff', 'defendant', 'preferred embodiment', 'inference', 'analogous field', 'burden of proof', and 'accused device.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow jurors to take notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit jurors to take notes during trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although concerns exist that good note-takers may dominate deliberations, research and experience favor allowing notes; instruct jurors that notes are for personal use only and should not be shared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long sidebar conferences and excusing the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize in-court interruptions and jury removals that confuse or distract jurors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include marking exhibits before trial, ruling on exhibits before trial starts, requiring notice of witnesses/documents, and having objections/legal matters raised outside regular trial hours to avoid juror confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shield jury from unnecessarily lengthy/complicated foundation laying
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect jurors from protracted or technical foundation testimony that is not necessary for their factfinding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit foundation that is lengthy or complicated to prevent juror fatigue or loss of focus (citation: SRI Int'l).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide an exhibit notebook for each juror
rubrics_metrics.description: Give each juror a notebook (from each side) containing the patent-in-suit and principal exhibits; include index/tabs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notebooks can also contain fact stipulations, preliminary instructions, witness lists, and glossaries of technical terms; supplement periodically during trial to help jurors locate materials easily (Judge Cohn and Schwarzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow jurors to ask questions (subject to screening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit jurors to submit questions during trial for clarification, screened by the judge and answered by the judge or witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge must screen for sense and rule on objections without revealing source; instruct jurors to ask only for clarification not to explore theories. Benefits: clarifies misunderstandings and may help attorneys improve presentations; filtering avoids prejudice (Schwarzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow jurors to discuss evidence during the trial (ongoing deliberations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit jurors to discuss the evidence with one another during the trial instead of confining deliberations to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This radical suggestion can enhance comprehension (and allow jurors to ask clarifying questions) but risks premature decisions before all evidence is presented; weigh benefits vs. risk of early verdict formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant reasonable jury requests for readbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow jurors reasonable requests to have testimony read back during deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitates accurate recollection of testimony; judge should accommodate reasonable requests (Schwarzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow periodic expository (non-argumentative) summations
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit each side to give periodic summations that explain rather than argue content as the trial progresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expository summations can address ambiguities quickly and enhance comprehension, but need monitoring to prevent counsel from using them to argue issues under the guise of exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruct counsel to remind witnesses to address jurors
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell counsel to direct their witnesses to speak to the jurors rather than the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses and lawyers often focus on the judge; directing testimony to jurors increases juror attentiveness (Judge Cohn and Schwarzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court retains exclusive duty to construe patent claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is a question of law for the court to decide after considering evidence (including extrinsic evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court must pronounce claim meanings as a matter of law (often in jury instructions or in dispositive motions); courts may use expert affidavits or testimony prior to trial to aid construction (Markman framework).

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold equitable defenses or try them in separate nonjury proceedings when restricting jury role
rubrics_metrics.description: If the court limits the jury to factual issues, it may order separate nonjury trials (prior or concurrent) for equitable defenses like inequitable conduct, laches/equitable estoppel, or patent misuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include separate prior nonjury trial, concurrent nonjury trial in morning/afternoon, or a separate nonjury trial after a jury trial if issues are intertwined (cases cited: Gardco; Aukerman; Yarn Processing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify questions of law typically reserved for the court
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues characterized as legal questions include enablement, indefinite claiming, claim construction, prosecution history estoppel, implied license, and repair vs. reconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are generally for the court to decide as law (citations to Federal Circuit decisions provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify questions of fact typically for the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact issues include utility, novelty (anticipation), original inventor, abandonment, inadequate description, best mode, literal infringement, doctrine of equivalents (and reverse DOE), lost profits, reasonable royalty, and willful infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are usually factual determinations for the jury to resolve, though some may have legal overlays; willfulness, while factual, may relate to judge's discretion for enhanced damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify hybrid legal issues based on underlying facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some legal determinations are based on underlying factual questions, including statutory subject matter, nonobviousness, and section 102(b) on-sale/public-use/printed-publication bars, and prior inventor issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are law questions requiring factual findings; courts should recognize the mixed nature and allocate responsibilities appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select appropriate form of verdict and draft it before trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The court has discretion over verdict form (special verdict, general verdict with interrogatories, or general multiple-part verdict); the form must be agreed before trial begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special verdicts or instructive interrogatories can illuminate decision-making. Plaintiffs prefer general forms; defendants prefer detailed forms. Good verdict forms should logically lead jurors through principal issues, use clear language, avoid leading questions, and be unbiased. Drafting forms before pretrial helps focus trial issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure jury instructions are legally correct and sufficiently comprehensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury instructions, read as a whole, must be legally accurate and sufficiently comprehensive to address disputed factual issues; no instruction should be given on a legal proposition lacking competent evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trial court must give meaningful instructions that jurors can understand and apply once factual disputes are resolved. Federal Circuit reviews adequacy for prejudicial legal error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give preliminary instructions describing patent system and issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide preliminary instructions that include a description of the patent system, an overview of rules on validity and infringement, what the parties agree and disagree on, and what jurors must decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary instructions orient jurors to the case's context and scope (Schwarzer; Judge Cohn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use written instructions and allow jurors to take copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Give jurors written instructions they may follow during the charge and take into the jury room; consider tape-recording the oral charge and providing a copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing written or recorded copies supports juror comprehension and retention (Cohn; Schwarzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider timing of substantive instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider delivering substantive instructions at the close of evidence and before arguments, and briefly re-instructing after closing arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Schwarzer advises giving substantive instructions near the end of evidence and a brief instruction after closings to reinforce duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate law with facts in instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use instructions that connect relevant legal principles directly with the facts jurors must find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration helps jurors apply law to evidence rather than treating instructions as abstract legal statements (Schwarzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid legal terminology and use psycholinguistic best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid jargon and use language proven to improve juror comprehension: concrete words, avoidance of homonyms and negative modifiers, simple grammar, and good organization of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psycholinguistic research supports plain-language instructions to reduce juror confusion and misapplication of law; examples of terms to avoid are provided (Charrow & Charrow; Elwork research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use model patent jury instructions as starting points
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider existing model instructions from bodies like AIPLA, Fifth/Ninth/Eleventh Circuits, District of Delaware, and collected instruction volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models vary widely; use them as a starting point but adapt to the case and prefer plain English versions (Delaware 'plain English' instructions recommended as basis in Appendix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft plain-English model instructions incorporating legal updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide model instructions written in plain English that incorporate recent statutory changes (e.g., GATT-implementing legislation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix provides such proposed instructions based on 1993 Delaware instructions and psycholinguistic research — use as templates to improve juror comprehension.
